speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY REPORT OF ADVISORY BOARD COMMITTEE AND CORRESPONDENCE WITH UNITED STATES GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
I would like to ask the right
hon. the Prime Minister whether, in view of what was said in his closing observations on the address in reply to the speech from the throne regarding the desirability of giving as little publicity as possible to the report of the advisory board in connection with the St. Lawrence waterway until certain matters had been dealt with, the time has not arrived when we might reasonably hope to have those papers laid before parliament, especially in view of the fact that a fairly well authenticated report prevails in Washington and also in Ottawa that a communication was sent by this government to Washington, to which a reply had been received. In view of that I suggest that perhaps the representatives of the people in parliament should have the opportunity to see these papers, and if the Prime Minister thinks the public interest would not be prejudiced, he might make some arrangement by which the members of this house would have some idea as to just what the situation is.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY REPORT OF ADVISORY BOARD COMMITTEE AND CORRESPONDENCE WITH UNITED STATES GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
As my hon. friend will recall, I mentioned in my remarks on the address that a communication had been sent by the government to Washington with reference to the St. Lawrence waterway project. That communication was not replied to until the end of last week. The reply, as a matter of fact, came into my hands only on Friday or Saturday last, and has not yet been communicated to my colleagues in the government. I would say, however, having read the reply, that I am very much of the view that it would scarcely be advisable to make public immediately either the communication which was sent to Washington or the reply which has been received.

It may seem that the government is seeking in some way not to inform the house fully. As to whether we are exercising wise judgment in that matter must be left, I think, until later when the communications themselves are brought down. A transaction of the character in contemplation, if it is ever to come to anything, cannot be surrounded with too many safeguards. While the government has exchanged communications wholly of a preliminary character, which in no particular bind the country' in any way, but which have been exchanged for the purpose of clearing the ground, so to speak, and in order that parliament may be fully informed of any possible basis of negotiations of a final character, should such ever be reached, it is inadvisable I think, and might possibly prejudice the outcome, too soon to present to parliament any of the documents in the matter. The government must take responsibility for withholding for the time being correspondence which it deems inadvisable to' have given to the public. We must be judged later on as to whether or not we have acted wisely. I have no doubt that when hon. members see the correspondence they will feel that the government was justified in not at present making public the two communications that have been exchanged.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY REPORT OF ADVISORY BOARD COMMITTEE AND CORRESPONDENCE WITH UNITED STATES GOVERNMENT
speechtext: I wholly appreciate the position taken by the Prime Minister, and he will observe that I asked whether or not in his opinion the time had arrived when we might receive the correspondence, because I realize that in the conduct of government those who direct it must exercise their best judgment and discretion as to whether the interests of the country would be best served by publicity or the retention of the documents in the hands of the government until the time is opportune. I only desired to ask if in the opinion of the Prime Minister that time had not yet arrived.

Mr. GEORGE H. PETTIT (Welland) moved that the House go into committee on Bill No. 14 to incorporate the Niagara Falls Memorial Bridge Company (as amended).

Mr. Speaker, before you declare the motion carried, I crave the indulgence of the house to place on record the opposition of the government of the province of Ontario to this bill, and also the opposition of the Niagara Falls Park Commission. The commission

1452	COMMONS
Niagara Falls Memorial Bridge
controls the 2,000 acres of park system from one end of the river to the other. It also controls the river bank and the land under the river up to the international boundary.
To me, Mr. Speaker, it is strange that the government should allow a bill of this kind to pass in face of the opposition of the provincial authorities. Of course, I shall be told that this is a private bill, but when it first appeared on the order paper it contained no declaration that the proposed bridge was a work for the general advantage of Canada, and the government having been instrumental in amending the bill in this respect, must take responsibility for it as a government measure. I say again, it is very strange to me that the government should fly in the face of the provincial government, which controls all the highways up to the bridges on the Niagara river, and, in effect, tell the government of Ontario that a charter is to be granted to this private company to erect a bridge over the river and on the park commission's land.
The opposition of the province of Ontario is not a factious opposition, but is based on sound grounds. The main reason for opposing the charter is that the bridge is not needed, and, further, that it will mar the scenic beauties of both the gorge and the falls. At the present time within a distance of six miles there are four bridges, one for railway traffic and the other three for vehicular and pedestrian traffic. In addition, there is a vehicular and pedestrian bridge at Buffalo, as well as a second railway bridge.
The engineer of the Niagara Falls Park Commission appeared before the private bills committee and gave evidence that the present bridges are capable of carrying 100 per cent more traffic; but the promoters did not call an engineer in support of their project.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Are the
present bridges privately owned?

Yes, they were built under federal charters. Those charters provide that the tolls to be charged are to come before the governor in council for approval. A new bridge was built last year, and the charter authorizing its construction contained a similar provision. I have inquired both of the Clerk of the Privy Council and of the Public Works department and have ascertained that nothing has been passed approving of the tolls that are being charged. Last year one these bridges under the purview of the federal parliament raised its tolls 100 per cent, without any redress whatever; and the only thing that can be done is to take drastic measures against this tendency. The people appealed to the 
parks commission who, by threatening those in charge with the possibility of some day having action taken to force their hands, got them to restore the tolls to the former figure. They were told that some day they might be wanting something and that they would not get it unless they put the tolls back where they were, and in that way they were forced to restore them.

Do I understand the hon.
member to say that the governor in council in this particular instance, when the tolls were raised, forced them to make the reduction?

They were not observing the charter. There was in the charter one of those weak kneed clauses providing that the governor in council should approve of their tolls. They never got them approved. They had been charging tolls for twenty years without getting them approved and they were therefore collecting these tolls illegally. But that is aside from the question. The province of Ontario does not want to be afflicted with another such institution. When it is time to have a bridge erected there the province may want to build it. Or this parliament might want to undertake the work. I can say that there is no better investment which anyone can make, and I do not want to see this matter left in private hands. I have seen too much of that sort of thing along the Niagara river. That is one of the reasons for cur objection.
As regards concessions on the river, as I said a moment ago, the parks commission, acting for the province of Ontario, have the whole river in their charge. They even have the power contracts in their charge. To show the value of the parks commission in the last forty years, I may say that the province of Ontario once gave the rights to a power concern for all the power in the Niagara river for $25,000 a year. Fortunately, the commission had a reasonable opportunity to cancel that agreement so that to-day the province of Ontario is receiving a rental from the commission of over $500,000 a year for a concession which originally was given away at $25,000. The province of Ontario has spent $7,000,000 on that front. I may give another illustration of what has been done in this regard. When I first went on the board fifteen years ago we were renting the Table Rock house concession to private individuals. At that time we were getting $4,000 a year and we raised it to $12,000 in a year or two. Those who were enjoying the concession complained and we replied:	"Very well; you
will not have it at all for we will run it ourselves." The result was that the first year

Niagara Falls Memorial Bridge
we made a profit to the province of $60,000, and last year on the same concession, with the fare reduced 50 per cent, we made a net profit of $125,000.
I object to this bridge on the public ground that, first of all, this parliament has no right to override the province. I am speaking now merely of its moral right. Parliament has no right to go over the heads of the commission; it has no right to give a private concession for money-making purposes over the property of the parks commission. We object further on this ground:	The improvements
which have already made over the present bridges will accommodate 100 per cent more traffic than before without any congestion. As a matter of fact, we know that the congestion last year was less than it was the year before and the year previous to that, and with heavier traffic. All that may be said to the contrary is that in a few instances, on a few days, there has been congestion. No one will dispute that. But we were met with that same objection when the bill was defeated in this parliament last year, and at that time we made a very close analysis of the situation. We put our engineers on the job and we took actual photographs of the scene every day last summer. We have those photographs arranged in order, some ten a day, covering the whole season, and we know just what days were crowded and on what days the traffic was light. There appeared before the committee a gentleman who gave us a couple of photographs-perhaps there were half a dozen of them-and he had the nerve to inform the committee that- these photographs were evidences of what happens every day at the bridge. That, of course, is idle talk; it is sheer nonsense. All I can say is that the people who came forward looking for the charter would say anything on earth in order to secure it. They even produced before the committee a sheaf of telegrams, together with a petition bearing 12,000 names. It will be intereseting to the house to know that these names obtained through the services of paid canvassers-ten cents a name. Oh yes; they did a good job. They even went to the schools and got the pupils from six to ten to sign the petition. No wonder they secured the number of names they did. That charge I made in the committee and it was not denied; nor can it be denied. I had a gentleman in the committee who gave evidence to the effect that his own boy had signed it. The school children ran home to their parents telling them, "We are going to have a new bridge; we have all signed the petition." Now, we in this house appreciate 56103-93i
the value of a petition: we also appreciate the value of telegrams sent in batches. The statement was made in the committee that, 4.000 persons from my constituency had signed the petition. I can say truthfully that not one person ever took the trouble to write to me even a note nor to send me a telegram, nor did anyone ever speak to me about the matter. They believed that I knew better than any of them did, what was needed there.
I am close to the Niagara bridge; my county takes in one of these bridges I have been discussing; and the next county is that of Welland. The parks commission, I may explain, comprises seven members, one from Lincoln, which is my county, three from Welland, one from Brant and two from Toronto, one of the commissioners from Toronto being the Minister of Highways in the provincial government. He is the seventh member. For the county in which Niagara Falls is situated, two of the members of the commission come from that city, and one comes from the same county, the same city, as the promoter of the bill, the member for the county of Welland. The commission, therefore, is unanimous; it was unanimous last year. They have presented a resolution which I want to put on record.
Is this bridge above or below the one which is closest to the falls?
This bridge, according to the plan submitted, is several hundred feet north of the bridge which is closest to the falls, the steel arch bridge.
Further down the river.

Yes. Now I will not say that this bridge may not be necessary in time, but w'hat we claim is that it is not necessary now, and from what we can see it will not be necessary for a number of years. But when it does become necessary to build a bridge, surely the parties to determine where it should be located are either the parks commission or the province of Ontario. I make that statement for this reason: the bridge should co-ordinate with the main highways, which are under the control of the province of Ontario. That is only reasonable. At present the government of Ontario are opposed to it because they feel the bridge is not needed.

Will my hon. friend allow me a question? Would he state to the house what authority he has for saying that the government of Ontario are opposed to the bill?

Niagara Falls Memorial Bridge

Mr. Speaker, I read to
the committee a letter from the Prime Minister, and I believe that should be conclusive evidence that the government are opposed to it.
opposed to it.

Mr. CANNON:
He did not say he was
Most decidedly he did. Oh, no.
I can also produce correspondence from the Minister of Highways in which he says he is strenuously opposed to it, and in which he asks me to oppose the bill.
Where is it?

Unfortunately I did not
bring either of these letters with me, but before I sit down I will have them, even if I have to detain the house a little longer.
My contention is that the position of this bridge should be determined by the province of Ontario, and while the Solicitor General has been good enough, to make some changes in the bill, in my opinion it does not give the province nearly enough authority in the matter. The Solicitor General does not seem to realize that we are just as much interested in the bridge as anyone, and I doubt very much whether any other government on this continent would dare pass legislation of this kind.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend if there is an objection to the location as well as to the bridge itself?
Absolutely.
Does the park extend down that far? Does it extend below the bridge which is already there?

I said a few moments ago, Mr. Speaker, that the park referred to by the hon. gentleman is 150 acres in extent. The park commission own 2,000 acres along the river; they own the whole bank of the river from one end to the other; they control for the province every foot of land from the source of the river to its mouth, and that is why we resent being told by this parliament where we shall have a bridge placed, when it shall be placed and that it shall be constructed by a private enterprise, which will collect money from the people of this country without paying a rental or anything of that kind. It is true that the companies owming the old bridges pay no rentals, but if the government were doing it all over again a thing of that kind would never be permitted; the government would collect money
TMr. Cannon.]
from them, as they should have had a right to do, for the granting of such a privilege. Why should you give anyone the right to build a bridge for which traffic has already been created, in order to permit people to make a big profit out of that sort of proposition? From everything along the river the park commission are collecting a revenue for the province of Ontario, and we are giving service at half the former cost. Last year, after carrying on all the work we had to do, we paid to the province $200,000, and in the last three years we have paid in $1,000,000.
Now I say to the government that after these circumstances were brought to their notice they had no business to grant a charter to a private company for this bridge. It is true that the charter contains a clause under which in time this bridge will come back to the province or to the Dominion. That is one of the things I tried to get the Solicitor General to tighten up in order to make it mean something, because as it is now all its teeth have been taken out. It might mean that when the Dominion took it over we would have to pay $400 a share or more for their stock. I suggested to the Solicitor General that a change be made to make sure that the bridge would be taken over at a reasonable price, as any stock would be retired, at say $100 or $105 or $110 per share, but in that regard he has not followed my advice.
As I have already said, the province has spent $7,000,000 on that frontier for the benefit of the people of the entire world, and we believe there are enough bridges in existence to take care of the present requirements. We object to another bridge being placed there first of all because it is not needed, and we brought evidence to that effect before the committee. Just at this point I wish to place on record a resolution which was passed by the park commission on February 28, of this year, to show their attitude in this connection:
Whereas the legislature of the province of Ontario by an act dated March 30, 1885, appointed commissioners for the purpose of selecting such lands in the vicinity of the falls of Niagara within Ontario as -were in their opinion proper to be set apart for the purpose of restoring scenic features to their natural condition and for the purpose of preserving the same from further deterioration.
And whereas the commissioners reported on September 18, and December 7, 1885, recommending that an area of about 154 acres of land be acquired by the province of Ontario along the Niagara river in the vicinity of the horseshoe or Canadian falls of Niagara for a public park with its management under provincial control.
And whereas the legislature passed an act on April 23, 1887, providing the means to establish, maintain, improve and develop the lands selected as and for a public park.

Niagara Falls Memorial Bridge
And whereas the park lands so selected, have, during forty years of effort and at an expenditure by the commissioners of over $7,000,000 to improve and beautify the same, been extended to include property bordering on the Niagara river from lake Erie to lake Ontario, all of which are declared by the park act to be public works of Ontario.
And whereas certain applications to the parliament of Canada are pending for acts to incorporate companies with power to construct, maintain, and operate bridges across the Niagara river within a distance of 800 feet from the upper steel arch bridge.
And whereas the upper steel arch bridge has been and is being greatly improved and extended as to its terminal facilities increasing its capacity on the American side four times and on the Canadian side 100 per cent.
And whereas the lower steel arch bridge has greatly extended its terminal facilities.
And whereas the increased means of access and exit appear to be ample not only for present requirements but for some distance into the future.
Now therefore be it resolved:
1.	That the Niagara Parks Commission is opposed to the construction of a new bridge in the vicinity of the upper steel arch bridge, because,
(1) it will mar the scenic beauty of the falls and park, and (2) it is not necessary to accommodate public travel.
2.	That the location of a new bridge, when required, should be midway between the two present traffic bridges below the falls, where it would not have so injurious an effect upon the scenic beauty of the falls and park, and also, m order that the traffic from the bridge terminals, may not, by their proximity create congestion.

passed?

It was passed on
February 28 of this year.

How many members were

There was a quorum of
the board; four of the seven members were present.

commission for Welland city present?

He was in Bermuda, .but
he left a 'letter to the effect that he was opposed to the bridge. Now I want to refer to a letter written by the Prime Minister of Ontario. I have here a letter written by him to the secretary of our commission under date of January 16, 192S. I might say that at this time we were fighting the bridge company for a reduction of tolls, and that will explain why the Prime Minister of the province made a reference to the matter.

speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend why, if the governor in council have authority to regulate the tolls, the matter was not referred to them.
First of all it was not the park commissioners' business; we had nothing to do with the bridge.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
But I am
speaking of the existing provision.

My answer to the hon.
gentleman is that we were out of our province in considering the matter at all. At that time I did not know that these clauses were in the charter, or that we had no control over these bridges. I only found that out when we got down here. When we got that information we took the means at hand of correcting the situation. Here is the Prime Minister's letter to Mr. Jackson, the engineer and general manager of the park.
I have before me yours of the 14th.
I am just as strongly opposed to the building of the additional bridge across the Niagara, as proposed, as I was last year, and for the same reasons.
The minister says the premier did not say so.
I think that the commission should use all its efforts to defeat any such project.
There is only one reason that would induce me to alter this view, that is, the necessity for relieving the public from being held up in the matter of fares by those who already hold franchises.
At the time the Prime Minister wrote that letter, the matter was in confusion. We had not succeeded in getting those tolls put back, but by the time we got here we had that matter rectified, without any reference here. It was only, as I explained before, when I came down here and had a chance to view the charters, that I found the clauses in question. The Solicitor General was good enough to tell me of them, because he had the charters in front of him. He told us how well he would look after these bridge companies in t-he future. Well, his predecessors had had the charters in their possession for twenty years, or more, and had not done so. I had confidence that we were better able to look after those matters than were such a dead bunch.

speechtext:
My hon.
friend is taking a great deal of credit to himself. He knew the proper court to come to for redress and yet he did not come.

speechtext: I think you had to do with them.

I do not know that you could get any stronger or more positive declaration than that.

It is dated March 3, 1928.
Mr. Henderson appeared before the committee.
Mr. Henderson appeared before the committee and made representations from the province strenuously opposing the bridge.
He did not.

Well if the Solicitor
General-
I will withdraw that remark. I will deal with it when I speak.

The statement of the
Solicitor General in regard to that is just ibout as correct as his statement about the ittitude of the Prime Minister of Ontario and ;he Minister of Highways whose letters I have [DOT]ead.
I now wish to place on record a communi-lation from the State Reservation Commission, a body on the other side of the river. This commission was appointed many years ago in order to do the same work in the state of New York that we were doing

in Ontario. Here is a letter dated March 12, 1928, from the president of the State Reservation Commission at Niagara.
That is the state of New York.

The state of New York. The letter is as follows:
Supplementing my letter to you of the 27th of March-
That is when this bill was up last year- 1927-
-of which I enclose a copy, I beg to say that the attitude of the State Reservation Commission at Niagara as expressed in that letter, is unchanged; that all of the considerations in it outlined militating against the construction of a new bridge apply with even greater force than then expressed.
Permit me to summarize for your consideration the underlying reasons moving our commission to oppose similar legislation when presented to the New York state legislature at Albany:
1st. The construction of a new structure such as proposed inevitably would be disastrous to the scenic grandeur of the great cataract, and the impressive gorge below. In this conviction we strongly are sustained by the well considered and strongly expressed opinion of the Hon. Frederick Law Olmstead, admittedly one of the most distinguished landscape artists now living, who was consulted by us upon this subject.
2nd. Such a structure seriously would interfere with the plans now under consideration by us for the expenditure of large sums of money, especially devoted by the people of our state to the further enhancement of the scenic grandeur and beauty of the cataract.
3rd. An important factor of our expenditure will he the elimination of conditions tending to impair and seriously to detract from the majesty of the cataract.
4th. There is not any need for an additional bridge. Whatever delays and congestion in traffic have arisen, has been infrequent, sporadic and entirely due to the rigorous inspection by the officials of the customs and immigration departments of both the Canadian government and our own.
As you are aware, there has been provided at the respective bridge heads additional lanes of traffic, which now are available for such inspection, more indeed, than those departments reasonably can be expected to utilize for many years in the future.
You are entirely at liberty to use this letter in any manner you see fit. Particularly shall I be pleased if you will present it to the Canadian parliament, or to any of its committees which may have this matter under consideration.
This is from the commission on the other side of the river.

a government bill. The hon. member for Lincoln has stated that this bill is sponsored and supported by the government as such in direct opposition to the views held by the government of Ontario in connection with the matter. Let us understand the real situation, in order that the impression may not be spread abroad that such a conflict between the two governments does exist in connection with this bill.
The province of Ontario was represented before the committee when the bill was under consideration, not by my hon. friend from Lincoln, but by Mr. Henderson, K.C., of the city of Ottawa, who held a brief for the Attorney General of Ontario, and so stated before the committee. Two weeks have elapsed since then. The representative of the Attorney General of Ontario has had that amendment in his hands ever since, and he has made no representations as to any further amendment. And why? Because, contrary to what the hon. member for Lincoln has asserted before this committee, the property neighbouring the Niagara river where the bridge if built is to lie, is to be dealt with in such a fashion that the rights of the province of Ontario will be safeguarded.
My hon. friend from Lincoln has said that we were doing away with all the rights of the parks commission of which he is a member. With all deference to my hon.
(Mr. Cannon.]
friend, and with all due respect to the splendid work which he has done as a member of that commission in the embellishment of that part of the Niagara district, I must say that his statement to the house exceeds a true picture of the facts.
The bill simply says this: The company may not build that bridge, may not locate the site of the bridge, and may not commence the work in order to complete the bridge, without first getting into touch with the commission of which my hon. friend is a member and agreeing as to t'he conditions on which the work is to be undertaken. The company shall not locate, construct or operate-

If my hon. friend will
follow me, first of all the company will have to get into touch with the parks commission and try and agree as to the conditions. That is provided in the last part of the clause which reads:
-and failing such consent, within sixty days from the date of the request made in writing by the company for such consent to the Queen Victoria Niagara Falls Park Commissioners, then upon such terms as are fixed by the board of railway commissioners for Canada.

Surely.
M'r. HEAPS:	The railway commission
would be the final arbiter, and not the parks commission at all?

The amendment covers

But failing such an agreement between the parks commission and the oompany, as this parliament always legislates for a practical object, and we have to foresee a possible deadlock, foreseeing that possible deadlock, we had to provide a remedy for it, and as a remedy we have chosen a perfectly impartial third body, the railway commission, which will decide the matter at issue, and either uphold the contention of the parks commissioners, or else prescribe1 the new conditions upon which the construction of the bridge shall take place.

The railway commission
will decide the conditions upon which the bridge is to be built; but they cannot decide that it shall not be built at all.
That is the whole story.

If my hon. friend will
allow me, the clauses of the bill deal with the different aspects of the undertaking, but always subject to the basic principle that parliament having adopted the preamble, considers that a second bridge should be built.

Is the ultimate
decision of the railway board entirely to govern the location?

Yes. Section 19 provides that the company Shall not locate, construct or operate except under certain conditions. This is in answer to my friend's first point, that the wishes of the province of Ontario were disregarded, and, secondly, that provincial rights were not safeguarded. Let me say that Mr. Henderson represented the government of Ontario before the private bills committee and made certain representations, and since the bill has been amended he has made no further representations, from which I think it may be inferred that he is satisfied with the bill in its present form. As to the rights of the province of Ontario, as represented by the park commissioners, not being protected, I submit with all deference that section 19 gives absolute right to the park commissioners, before any work is started, to discuss with the company certain conditions, and if the company is unreasonable, then the railway board will consider the whole situation; and I have enough confidence in the railway board to believe that justice will be done.

I do not think anyone
will dispute the Solicitor General's statement that the railway board will endeavour to do justice. But once this bill is passed the company have a statutory right to go ahead and construct the bridge, and when it fixes on a certain point where the bridge should tie up with the land, is not the railway board bound to give a decision that will permit the construction of the undertaking? It must give a decision permitting the undertaking to proceed.
Not necessarily; otherwise section 19 would be senseless.
It may be senseless.

I say it would be senseless, because the power of the railway board would be restricted to such an extent that it would simply be illusory. But it is not so restricted. Section 19, if I understand it

rightly, provides, in effect, that the company having power to locate, construct and maintain, will not exercise that power without previously obtaining the consent of the park commisisoners, upon conditions to be arranged, and failing such consent, the matter may be referred to the railway board. But the railway board
will not have power to say that the bridge shall not be built.

Certainly they will not
have power to say the bridge shall not be built; but they will have power to say: first, your bridge shall be built on a certain site; second, you shall construct your bridge under certain conditions; third, you shall maintain your undertaking under certain conditions. The railway commission
will not have authority to say to the company after this bill passes: you shall not build that bridge at all.

We are only playing with
words.
No.

Will the Solicitor General permit me one further question? Clause 7 is the empowering clause, and it says clearly that the bridge shall ,be constructed:
At or near a point between the property of the Canadian National Railways on River road and the north limit of Bender street in the city of Niagara Falls in the county of Welland in the province of Ontario, to a point in the city of Niagara Falls in the state of New York.
Now then, if the bridge is located at any point within that area, the railway board cannot impose conditions that will prevent the company from constructing the work. The Solicitor General will admit that?

I will admit that the
location of the bridge will have to be within the four corners of section 7.

And that the railway
commission cannot withhold their consent if the bridge is between those points?

I would not say that. I
suppose the hon. gentlemen who represent these localities could furnish the committee better information on these points than I possess, but if I understood rightly the discussion before the committee there is quite a lot of space where a bridge could be built.

But the location is
specified in the bill.

Section 7 says between
such point and another point. Let me give the exact words:
7. The company may construct, maintain and operate a bridge across the Niagara river for the passage of pedestrians, vehicles, cariages, electric cars or street cars and for any other like purpose, with all necessary approaches, from a point at or near a point between the property of the Canadian National Railways on River road and the north limit of Bender street in the city of Niagara Falls in the county of Welland in the province of Ontario,-
That is one point.

The hon. members who
represent these constituencies are in a much better position than I can possibly be to give information to the committee.

Yes.
-to a point in the city of Niagara Falls in the state of New York, one of the United States of America,-
That is, as far as the bridge is concerned, we have to consider the Canadian side; in other words, we can legislate only in so far as Canada is concerned. As to the American side, it will be for the proper authorities there to deal with the matter. On the Canadian side, we say: we empower you to build the bridge from that point to this other point, but as to the exact location of the bridge, this must be agreed upon between yourselves and the park commissioners before the work is started, and failing such agreement, the location will be decided by the railway board. I will come to that. I
pass now to my second point. The hon. member (Mr. Chaplin), with great ability and also with the experience he has derived from many years of service on the commission, has told the committee that this is an attempt on the part of certain private interests to get from

parliament the power to build a bridge over the Niagara river and to exact tolls from the public. It is a bridge owned by a private company, whose representatives when they appeared before the committee refused to address them. When I asked the question as to what was the financial standing of the company for the last twelve months and what their revenues had been no answer was given. If my hon. friend did not use that term I will correct myself. I say, it is not correct that too say that the company is trying to secure authority to build a bridge which would be a gold mine. Now, let us examine the facts.

I am coming to that.

I thought my hon. friend

However, as a member of the committee, I may say that there appeared before us the mayor of Niagara Falls-
Who is also a promoter of the bill, one of the officers of the bridge company asking for the charter.
My hon. friend is a member of the parks commission and it is his right to state his views. The mayor of Niagara Falls came forward in regard to another bridge-

service.

Falls appeared in his official capacity. Before I go any further, let me say that I am not criticizing my hon. friend from Lincoln for being a member of the commission, but I am very much surprised, in view of the high character of the gentleman who fills the office of mayor of Niagara Falls that the hon. member should try to discredit him by saying that he is interested in this bridge. Mr. Stephens appeared before the committee and I do not think that in anything he said he gave occasion for my hon. friend to insinuate that he was interested. He appeared on behalf of the municipality of Niagara Falls; other gentlemen appeared also. They represented, first, that a second bridge was necessary ; they pointed out that the necessity arose by reason of considerable congestion of traffic. In the second place, they contended that it was necessary on account of exorbitant tolls which had been charged by one existing bridge. And in the third place, in support of the contention that the construction of the new bridge was urgent, they submitted a petition signed by many thousands of people. I as a member of the committee felt convinced that the people who live in that locality were very anxious that second bridge should be built.
A second one? You mean a fourth.
My hon. friend knows that only one bridge can be used now for ordinary traffic in automobiles and pedestrians, the arch bridge.
I know no such thing; that statement is not correct. I do not know whether the Solicitor General is aware of the situation or not. He knows nothing about it if he persists in that statement.

I will leave the question to the committee; I do not think it would be much use arguing with my hon. friend considering the tone he has adopted. The committee had evidence before them that the people living in that locality, who after all are the people who should know the real conditions, supported the proposal. I wish now to call the attention of the committee to a third point. If hon. members will read care-

fully Bill No. 14 as reprinted and amended, they will see that we have surrounded the provisions of the bill with every possible precaution in order to safeguard what we consider to be the public interest. I would ask hon. gentlemen to glance at clauses 7, 8, 10, 14, 16, 17, 18 and 19. In all these clauses we have given authority to the governor in council to supervise and control the operations of the company, should that company be allowed to build a bridge.
Before concluding, let me say that as a member of the government I immediately realized, when I attended that committee, the serious danger which might lie in empowering a private company to build toll bridges, not only at Niagara Falls but at other points on the international frontier. I realized that it was my duty as a member of the government and as a member of the house to make it clear that these powers, if granted to a private company, were to be granted in such a way that the public interests of the citizens of this country should be properly protected. We insterted a clause in the bill, and although the hon. member for Lincoln has stated that the clause has no teeth, I would ask hon. gentlemen to examine it; it is clause 18. Under that clause, when the company constructing the bridge have redeemed their corporate obligations, the bridge then becomes the property of the Dominion government or of any other government or public body designated by the federal government.
Perfectly meaningless.

My hon. friend says that
is perfectly meaningless.

Show us the teeth in
it.

I will do so in just a
moment. If my hon. friend would credit me with some interest in the welfare of the citizens of this country he might realize that I would not take it upon myself to insert such a clause without being sure first that that clause had an object and secondly that the object was possible of attainment. My hon. friend from Lincoln rightly stated that in reading the original bill that clause would not be of any use because the financial obligations of the company might be so excessive that the day would never come when they would be properly discharged. Having this in view, and having also examined with care the United States legislation covering the same subject matter, I inserted amendments all through the bill under which the governor general in council has absolute control over the financial operations of the company. When that com-
pany undertakes to transact any financial business which might have any bearing on section 18, the previous consent of 'the governor general in council will have to be secured. Moreover, in order that we might not be met with the suggestion, should this government consider it in the public interest to take over this bridge, that we were infringing upon vested rights, I would refer hon. members to section 21, which I inserted and which provides that the right to alter, amend or repeal this act is expressly reserved.
To whom?

To the authority which
has legislated; when a reservation of any legislative power is made, evidently that reservation is in favour of the authority which has enacted the legislation wherein the reservation is to be found. It is true that parliament is a supreme authority and has the right to repeal, amend or alter any legislation which it passes, but that authority is implied. As members of the committee we went further, and instead of simply having an implied authority under which we could act we made it an express authority by inserting that clause in the act.
In conclusion may I say that when this and another bill concerning a bridge at Sarnia were before the committee, I was impressed with the fact that none of the companies operating the other bridges at Niagara Falls have submitted their tolls to the governor in council, although it is stated in their charters that that must be done. Before the committee I made a statement which I now repeat, that that situation will have to be dealt with in order to protect the public, and the tariff of tolls must be submitted to the governor in council. In this bill which we are now considering I refer the committee to section 10, which reads as follows:
The company may charge tolls for the use of the said bridge, approaches and facilities, and may regulate the tolls to be charged: Provided that such tolls shall have been previously approved by the governor in council. . . .
I added the word "previously" to the words which were to be found in the former legislation, in order to make sure that the tariff would not be exigible until approved by the governor in council. Not only have we the right to examine the tolls before the company has a right to charge such tolls, but section 10 contains a further item which gives the governor in council power to revise these tolls from time to time, and the section further states that the tolls shall be equal to all persons using the bridge, approaches and facilities.

Niagara Falls Memorial Bridge
To sum up, section 10 says first that the company will have to submit their tolls to the governor in council for approval before those tolls can be charged the public, and it also provides that if the governor in council sees that a revision would be useful, the governor in council will have the right to revise those tolls.

speechtext: Order. My hon. friend has exhausted his forty minutes.

I think the Solicitor 'General has covered the ground rather thoroughly, but for fear there may be some misapprehension as to the location of this bridge I would call attention to section 7 of the bill. Under that section this bridge will be located at a point from 800 to 1,000 feet north of the present upper steel arch bridge, away from the falls. There is a spread of 200 feet there, and of course you cannot put your finger right on the spot where the bridge will be constructed, but it will be within those limits.

While my friend is on
that subject, will he tell me how far the Canadian National property is from the upper steel arch bridge?

I would imagine it is from
400 to 600 feet away.

You know very well it
is only 250 feet.
I did not know that.

I know it, and you know
it now.

I want to tell the committee that no one in this house respects provincial rights as strongly as I do, but this bill does not infringe upon provincial rights except in so far as the parks commission, which is a creature of the provincial government, may be concerned. The park commission are only concerned with this 66-feet strip of roadway that passes along the edge of the gorge where this bridge is to touch. Now the bridge simply crosses the gorge, goes up to and against the side of this road and opens on to it. That is all that happens, nothing more or nothing less. So that there is no interference in any way with provincial rights, or any rights in which the park commission are concerned.

Could you not get a
charter from the provincial government for this bridge?

Absolutely no. This is a
matter beyond the jurisdiction of the province. The bridge will span the international boundary, and therefore will come within the jurisdiction of the Dominion.
Are there any objections to it from the province of Ontario?

If my hon. friend had been here he would have heard an objection by the Premier of the province of Ontario. I am glad the hon. member asked me that question because it will be noticed that the Premier of Ontario in his letter says: " I am against the building of this bridge for the same reason that I was last year." Now the reason why he was against the building of the bridge last year, and the reason why I opposed it also last year, was because the location of the bridge at that time was between the present bridge and the falls.

In his letter he did not
say " reason". He said " reasons".

I have mentioned one reason. The other reason was that it would mar the beauty of the scenery of the falls I agree that the former location would have had that effect because the bridge would have been between the present structure and the falls. But the contemplated bridge will be 800 or 1,000 feet farther away from the falls, and it will not mar the scenery one iota. The New York state end of the bridge will open out on private property which is an eyesore. But those dilapidated buildings will be expropriated and tom down and a nice entrance made. With this eyesore removed the scenery will be improved rather than marred. Certainly as far as the Canadian end of the bridge is concerned there will be no marring whatever of scenery. The bridge will simply come up to the road and will open out on to it. I have seen the plans of the proposed bridge and it will be a most artistic structure. The bridge will be very wide and will at least provide for six lines of automobiles, three going one way and three going in the other direction. The present situation is such that a new bridge is an absolute necessity. Notwithstanding the remarks of my hon. friend from Lincoln the congestion there is simply terrific. Not only on holidays, but throughout the tourist season of three months, that situation prevails, it being less on some days and on other days greater. The present upper bridge was built some 33 years ago when automobile traffic was unknown. Hon. gentlemen all realize the extent of that traffic to-day, and bearing in mind that this bridge cannot be constructed
Niagara Falls Memorial Bridge

or completed within two and a half years, they can form some idea of the enormous traffic which will have developed by the end of that period. Niagara Falls at that point is getting a black eye throughout the United States because of the present congestion of traffic. The automobile traffic is held up there for a period of anywhere from two to six, eight or even ten hours. People are ceasing to cross at that point and are crossing at other points. Personally I cannot understand the attitude of my hon. friend and the park commission in allowing that state of affairs to continue. I should have thought they would have welcomed the construction of another bridge, which would draw more people to that particular point, because it would mean thousands of dollars to the park commission in revenue from concessions, and the easier and the quicker the crossing, could be made, the greater number of tourists you would attract, with larger profit to the town, and millions of dollars to the province and the Dominion at large.
I have in my possession some 60' or 70 telegrams from leading business men, councils, boards of trade and other organizations. I produced these before the committee and if I were to read them now hon. gentlemen would realize in what strong language they are couched. The gist of these communications is that the congestion is great, it must be relieved at once, and the present monopoly broken. There are two bridges there.
The minister said there was only one.

The upper bridge will be about 800 feet away, and another bridge a mile and a half or a mile and three quarters farther away again. There is another bridge seven miles away from that, and the.fourth bridge is twenty miles distant, opposite Buffalo and Fort Erie. The large upper bridge had certain rates in force, and a year ago last October raised those rates 100 per cent. They were maintained at that figure until just about four weeks ago, when they were somewhat reduced but not to the original figures. So that instead of encouraging we are trying to break the existing monopoly. These two bridges have been there for years, they yield good returns, and naturally the owners want to keep the traffic and the revenues derived therefrom. The situation is such that something must be done to relieve the existing congestion, and to fix reasonable rates for the travelling public.
Are the other two bridges in the hands of private companies?

Yes. And as has been
pointed out by the Solicitor General, it was agreed by the promoters of the present bill that the proposed structure should become the joint property of both governments at the end of a certain period. This bill is an illustration of what may result from what has become an unfortunate habit or practice of parliament. One of the habits of parliament, not necessarily a rule, is to allow private bills to get their second reading without very much scrutiny. Very frequently they are put Through and sent to a committee on the plea, "Ch, well, the committee will give this bill consideration." But then when the bill comes back to this house we find ourselves confronted with a situation which implies, if it does not assert, that parliament is more or less committed to the principle of the bill, and all we are permitted to do is to consider its individual clauses.
In t'he first place, I should like to call attention to this fact, that the bill contains the well-known constitutional clause declaring the works and undertaking of the company to be for the general advantage of Canada. This means that the ' bill must receive the careful consideration of parliament as a whole, and that we should not be influenced by the wishes of a particular community, no matter how deserving or importunate that community may be. Now, the Solicitor General intimated that the bill is strongly supported by the mayor and certain other influential citizens of the town where the bridge is to be located, and this he advanced as a very strong argument why we should pass the bill with apparently very little scrutiny. I submit that we are clothed with a national responsibility, and that this imposes upon us the duty of scrutinizing the bill in detail independently of the wishes of those who may most benefit from it. We should, as a matter of fact, while listening courteously to their request, regard the bill from the standpoint of the general interests of Canada. That, I think, is a principle that we ought to apply in dealing with this measure.
The proposal presents many difficulties to me. I may say to my hon. friend who is sponsor for the bill that nothing would please me better than to get behind him and support his proposal; but when I realize that it involves the construction of a bridge across the international boundary, and, further, that in some measure it infringes on the rights of a public body such as the park commissioners, then I conceive it to be my duty to examine the bill very carefully. If the public interests cannot be properly safeguarded within the ambit of this measure then such a clause should not be put in. Furthermore I say that if the clause is effective, which I do do not believe it is, no solicitor for a bond company would ever pass the bonds which would be issued under that act. He would not pass them for a bonding company, my legal friends around me would not pass them. There is no solicitor for a bonding company, or for the trustee of the bondholders, who would ever approve of the issue of bonds with that clause in the bill without anything on the face of the bond to indicate to every bond purchaser that their bonds may be cancelled, or the rights of the company may be cancelled without notice. I say that the bonds would be unsaleable, and the raising of capital under those conditions would be a fruitless task. I believe I know something of what would happen because I have been in the financial end of the business for a good many years, and I know perfectly well the public would not take up bonds of this character.

Why should my hon.
friend object to the clause?
I object to the clause because it is a piece of nonsense to put it into the bill, if what I say is correoct.
Thank you for your judgment.
I may appear to the Solicitor General to be not very respectful of his views, but I do not know what impelled him to put the clause in.

I gave the reason a
moment ago.

I have argued the question from my standpoint, and I am convinced that what I have said is correct. I repeat that argument briefly: I do not think the clause is operative in the manner in which it is proposed to be enacted. If it is opera-

tive then I say the bonds are unsaleable. That is the point I make. I say further to the committee that if we are going to pass this legislation then we ought to safeguard the public interests in some other way than the inclusion of a clause of that character. I say very candidly that if I approved o'f this bill I would fight tooth and nail for the removal of that clause, because I would conceive it was not in the interest of the project at all, making it an inoperative and innocuous thing.
The discussion has been pretty well distributed over the clauses of the bill. I presume we are on clause 1, but I thought I should give the committee my views on the bill and state my opposition to the incorporation of this company under clause 1 so as to bring myself within the rules of the house.
Do I understand the preamble is carried?

The preamble carries last
in the house, but of course in the private bills committee it carries first. We are on clause 1, Whi'ch seeks to incorporate the company, and I am opposed to the incorporation of that company for the reasons I have outlined.

If I may venture a remark or two, I would say that the gentlemen whose names are mentioned in this bill are men of high standing in the community of Niagara Falls and the character of every one of them is above reproach.

I do not question that
for a moment. I want hon. gentlemen to understand that -clearly.

These gentlemen have
associated themselves together for the -purpose of carrying out this enterprise, and have come -before the house with this bill. As member for the constituency within which this -bridge is to be built I support it very strongly because of the intolerable condition of affairs that exists at Niagara Falls, owing to the congestion of traffic and the high rates now charged. The people of the community are bound to break that monopbly and to get some legislation from parliament that will relieve the existing state of affairs. In this effort they should receive the support of the province of Ontario, and of the federal government representing the country as a whole, because both are interested. I want to assure hon. members that I am as strong a supporter of public ownership as any other hon. gentleman here, but to those who suggest that either the province of Ontario or the Dominion should undertake this work, I

Niagara Falls Memorial Bridge
rejyly that neither the province nor the Dominion is going to undertake the building of bridges. Where would these two legislative bodies be if they undertook work of that character? Why, they would be at the beck amd call of every constituency in every part of the country. It is simply drawing a red herring across the trail to raise a point of that kind.

I should like to know if there is any difference in principle between the government of this province or the government of Canada building the bridge and the governments of the United States and Canada undertaking to construct jointly the St. Lawrence waterways scheme?

No, I do not see the
difference, and I am not opposing any such plan. But what are we going to do in the meantime while the respective governments are considering the matter?
Have you asked the government to build a bridge?

No, we have not asked this government to build a bridge. We are asking for authority to build it. We maintain that its construction is necessary in the public interest, to end an intolerable situation. This company is not acting from philanthropic or charitable motives. It wants to build the bridge and make a reasonable amount on the investment within such a period of time as would enable the cost of construction to be paid off. Then it is willing that this work shall become the joint property of both governments. I tell hon. gentlemen that this bridge is a necessity. The present congestion is simply intolerable, and it occurs not only on holidays but throughout the tourist season. I have been there and have viewed the conditions for myself. The gentlemen who sent these telegrams that I have in my hand -members of municipal councils and boards of trade, including Niagara Falls, the township of Stamford, the township of Willoughby, the township of Bertie, the town of Bridge-burg, the town of Fort Erie, and others- surely are not misrepresenting matters to this parliament. They tell you in no uncertain terms and very strong language, in the resolutions and telegrams they have forwarded, that the congestion cannot be endured any longer. Relief must be provided and the *existing monopoly must be broken. That is not only in the interest of the particular locality affected, but in the interests of the Dominion at large.

I should ljke to ask the
Solicitor General a few questions on this matter. Some provision is made in this bill for the stock of the company passing into the hands of the government. How would the United States regard the ownership of the bridge passing into the hands of what it might term a foreign country, and how would that affect the relations existing between the two countries? Would not the United States or the state of New York expect that in the passage of any legislation in which they were interested their rights should be safeguarded?

I may say first that no
international bridge has as yet become the property of the Dominion government, and that may be why we would like in the future to have such bridges come under the federal authority so far as Canadian interest in them is concerned. As to the hon. member's second question, I may say that the United States certainly cannot oppose that provision of our law because they have a similar provision in their legislation dealing with international bridges, and, thirdly, I do not see how this could affect our relations because the ownership of these bridges would be a co-ownership between the Canadian government or any Canadian authority which would be designated and the United States government or any other United States authority designated by that government. Instead of lessening friendly relations, I think it should increase them.

Supposing the United
States inserted in regard to this bridge exactly the same provisions which we are inserting in this bill, making it subject to orders in council they might pass, how would that affect us? Would that cause an impasse? Why should we be subject to their changes by order in council?

In considering all this
legislation, we must not lose sight of the fact that we are dealing with international waters and can legislate only covering the Canadian section, leaving to the United States authorities the duty of legislating in respect to the United States section. The necessity of cooperation in the way of legislation is imposed upon us by the very location of the bridge.

Does the stock issued
under this bill not cover the whole bridge?

No. We are incorporating the Canadian company; but in the act which incorporates the Canadian company there is a provision that the Canadian com-

pany may incorporate with a company which will receive its existence from a United States authority, and the two companies being amalgamated or combined, a third company will operate the bridge.

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Just before the committee rose I was about to reply to a question in respect to capitalization and profits on the bridge which in my judgment had been more or less imperfectly answered. It is quite true that as far as the Canadian end is concerned, all we can do is to incorporate a company for the purpose ,of handling one-half the bridge, and the same thing has to be done with respect to the other half in the United States. After that, there can be several ways of handling the matter. In one case it is handled by the two bridge companies meeting together on equal terms; in another case it is handled by a single corporation which gathers together the two bridge companies into a holding company.
As to the question of profits, so that there will be no misunderstanding, if there is one objection I have more than another it is that a bridge of this kind is a very profitable undertaking; there is no doubt about that. The new bridge that was put up at Buffalo has within seven months paid the whole year's expenses of the bridge-its sinking fund, the total interest on its investment, and salaries for the whole year-and shown a profit besides; and the five months left will give them an extra profit. So you can readily understand why a private corporation wants to get a bridge charter. It is for the laudable purpose of making money, and that is largely the ground upon which I am opposed to this bridge. We have made a mistake before, but what has been done cannot be remedied. There are two or three companies now operating and making large profits; I know whereof I speak. One of these companies paid 18 per cent on an enlarged capital, and in addition put aside more money than it paid out. Now I ask the committee if they think that the clause the minister has been discussing is ample in its provisions to protect the people of the country. If these bridge people come here with the idea of giving something away, let us see that what they intend to give reaches us; it is not going to reach us under the clause as it stands. This is the way it will work out under the bill as it is now before us: As the bridge is operated, gradually the mortgages and the bonds [Mr Cannon.]
will be retired. That immediately leaves more money for the stock, more money to be divided amongst the shareholders, who will be scattered all over the country, and they will be paid increasing rates of dividend; no doubt about that. As they get those increasing rates of dividend, because of the bonds and mortgages being retired and there being more money to go to the stock, the price of the stock will rise, and what I am asking the minister to do, if he means what he says, is to put a provision in the bill that at no time will more than 110 be paid for the stock. If he will do that, he will get away from any idea of profiteering on the bridge, and with that proviso I shall be satisfied wiith that particular clause. But I say frankly I am not satisfied with the bill. The bridge is useless, it is not needed, it is a money-making venture where we have enough bridges on that frontier already.
I wonder if those who are favouring this bill can tell me why this bridge is called a memorial bridge.

It is called a memorial
bridge in commemoration of the one hundred years of peace that has existed between the two countries, and also because it was thought the word memorial would be suitable in the jubilee year of confederation. The name is appropriate; that is all.
Would you consider offering that name to the pons asinorum?
If that suits you, all right.

I rise to a point of order,
Mr. Chairman. We are supposed to be discussing clause 1. The last three speakers have been talking either of clause 19 or of the title. On section 7-Powers. Construct bridge across Niagara river, etc.

Mr. Chairman, this is
the important section of the bill, for it authorizes the construction of a bridge across the Niagara river. Parliament is exercising its powers to create a company for this purpose because it happens to be am international waterway that is to be spanned; otherwise the matter would be dealt with by the legislature of Ontario. The powers granted to construct the bridge are made subject to legislation to be passed by congress or by the legislature of New York state. It is therefore apparent that this is not an absolute but a conditional power that is being -conferred. I observe from the public press that the legislature of the state of New York has recently declined to incorporate this company. I made inquiries and one hon. member told me that this is correct. Therefore we are now placing upon the statute books an act to incorporate a company that is to function conditionally upon the legislature of the state of New York granting similar powers, which, as I say, it has -refused to grant.

May I ask if the legislature
of New York state gave any reasons for refusing to incorporate the -company?

As I understand it, they
voted the bill down because they considered it to "be not in the -public interest. My authority for that is what I sa-w in the public press, and I assume my hon. friend saw it as well. May I direct the attention of the committee to the wording of the section?
-but the company may, in the meantime, acquire the lands, submit their plans to the governor in council, and do all other things authorized by this act.
I ask the committee if it is proper for us to say: although the corporate powers -may not be exercised unless and until the legislature of a foreign -country passes concurrent legislation with respect to the other end of the bridge, we will empower this -com-pany to seek subscriptions from the public and then buy land and do other things. In other words, this -com-pany may never be able to build the bridge. To pass such legislation would be to -take a course that I have never seen this or any other parliament take.
Let me come to another point. F-or years the city of Calgary has been trying to induce the Minister of the Interior to grant -powers to a local company to operate a power plant at Spray lakes in Banff national park. We were told that this would interfere with the scenic beauties -of the national park, which contains several millions of acres of land. Recently regulations were imposed -preventing even a prospector from operating any mineral claim within that area-again i-n order to preserve the scenic beauties. The land that would -be affected is far removed from the average traveller who visits the park. Furthermore, an application was recently made by one of the railway companies to acquire a mountain top in the province of British Columbia as a site for -bungalow camps. I have a telegram this morning from some friends the -proposal vitally affects the district of Banff, and they are very anxious that these bu-ngaloiY camps should be permitted- advising me that the deputy -minister of the Department of the Interior has been urging the British Columbia authorities not to grant this concession.
