speechtext:
That is
entirely wrong.

I am glad to hear it,
because it seems to me that if my information is correct Mr. Cory was exceeding his authority. Shall this parliament, exercising its powers purely as trustees, it being the only authority that can create a company to build this bridge because it is to span an international waterway presumably for the benefit of the people of Canada, but which

Niagara Falls Memorial Bridge
company cannot come into being unless a foreign power passes concurrent legislation- shall this parliament create such a corporation to traverse public parks and interfere with the scenic beauty of an area that is visible to the whole surrounding community, notwithstanding the opposition of the government of the province of Ontario as well as of the parks commission? It was said this afternoon that the Attorney General of Ontario could not have been very much in earnest because he was given an opportunity to submit another amendment and failed to do so. His answer is obvious, as communicated to me-he could not have anything to do with any such amendment because thereby he would be accepting the principle of this measure to which, on behalf of the province, rightly or wrongly, he is opposed.
It notwithstanding the objection of the province of Ontario we are to create this bridge company, le^ us at least provide that these powers shall not be exercised in the province without the consent of the provincial government. Is that an unreasonable request to make? My hon. friend the Minister of the Interior has for four years refused to grant power rights in the Banff national park because the government of the province of Alberta will not consent. He says, and very properly, that the provincial government in that case must determine the matter, the federal authority exercising its powers simply as trustees. Now, this parliament is enjoying jurisdiction in this matter merely because as I have already said, it happens to be, an international waterway that is to be spanned. That being so, let us exercise our power in such a way at least as will be consistent with the duty that rests upon us with respect to the province in which the bridge is to be built. That duty is to see that since the people of the province do not desire the bridge we should not charter a company to construct it. In other words, the company can derive corporate existence only from this parliament, but the exercise of its corporate powers, conditional1 as they now are upon concurrent legislation by congress or other competent authority in the United States, should also be subject to the further condition, namely, the consent of the province of Ontario. Does my hon. friend say that this is a precedent to enable him to deal with public lands and parks and grant leave to some to prospect for minerals and to others to exploit water powers in Alberta that he has refused during all these years because the government of that province was not agreeable? Is there anything more than that in this precedent? It

does seem to me that we are not dealing merely with the principle of this bill, we are in reality dealing with the principle of any bill from whatever province it may come, as long as the subject matter would be solely within the jurisdiction of the provincial authorities were it not for the fact that an international waterway is involved. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that we should not confer the powers sought by this bill unless and until the provincial authorities give their consent. They are better judges than we of what is in the public interest in this matter with respect to that province; they are better able than we to determine the necessities of the case. Who are we, sitting in Ottawa, dealing with national problems affecting the country as a whole, that we should determine what local interests are involved in that particular province in respect of this question? Not until that province itself has expressed its willingness and give its consent should this act become operative and the powers conferred by it become exercisable. That is the position that should be taken; and any declaration that make^ this a work for the general advantage of Canada, made by this parliament under the powers conferred upon it by the British North America Act, is wholly at variance with the general principles which heretofore have governed in matters of this kind. Here we are dealing with a private enterprise which seeks legislative sanction from the parliament of Canada merely because the legislature of the province of Ontario has not the power to grant that sanction. I say therefore that if we give our approval with respect to that incorporation, and confer upon it the right to charge tolls and thereby obtain revenues, we are departing from the established practice; it is not customary for the Dominion government to declare a work such as this to be for the general advantage of Canada. I admit that instances may be found in some of the statutes wherein this is done, but those who have given the subject the most careful consideration are agreed that in these cases the declaration should not have been made. That declaration is made with respect to railways-operated for profit it is true-as well as with respect to other utilities of that sort; but these are under the regulatory power of the railway commission or of some other competent body; and in any case they are enterprises that serve more than one province and touch the borders of more than one section of the Dominion. That is the general situation. There may be exceptional conditions that justify a particular work being declared for the general advantage of Canada, when it is international in character. So far

Niagara Falls Memorial Bridge
as this matter is concerned, however, it seems to me that the committee should approach the consideration of it with very great care. Apparently the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) is of the opinion that this legislation should be enacted; he declared this afternoon that it was not in any sense a government measure. But while that is true it must be borne in mind that no one but the government can take the initative in having it declared that this undertaking is of national significance; without the consent of the federal government no undertaking can be declared for the general advantage of Canada. That is axiomatic with respect to the exercise of the constitutional powers to which I have referred. I need hardly say that I have no interest in the enterprise, but the principle involved is one from which this parliament should not lightly depart. That principle is this: When we are dealing with a matter wholly provincial in its aspects, affecting the people of one province-and the people of Ontario are profoundly affected by this proposed legislation-interfering with the scenic attractions and natural beauties of their park, unless and until that province concurs, these powers should not be exercised. And if it is deemed wise to make the exercise of these powers subject to a condition, namely, that action shall first have been taken by a foreign congress or legislature, much more should we insist that the powers be not exercised unless the people of the province directly affected have given their approval. This is not a political matter, I trust; I trust also that it will not in any sense divide parties, for my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) and my hon. friend from Welland (Mr. Pettit) are poles apart in their attitude to the question. Since, however, it has been determined that the power of this parliament shall be exercised-and there is a majority to carry out that determination-let us at least hedge the exercise of that power with such limitations and conditions and such safeguards as will enable us to say that no principle has been departed from and that, to use the language of the United States, the sovereign rights of the people of Ontario have not been sacrificed by this parliament for any purpose whatsoever.

In answer to what the
leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) has said, may I point out that section 7 does not in any way indicate that the legislation enacted by this parliament shall be subject to any legislation that might be introduced either in the American congress or in any state legislature in the United States. That
is not the idea. This parliament is supreme within its own competence and can legislate as it sees fit. But not only have we these sovereign powers of legislation; we must exercise them in a practical way. We are now dealing with a proposed international bridge and we can confer powers for the construction only of half of that bridge. We must bear in mind always, therefore, what may be done so far as the other half is concerned; and this being so I think it is only common sense for this parliament to enact a provision that the powers conferred by this legislation shall not be exercised until we know what has been decided by competent authority on the other side, so as to obviate the possible eventuality of a Canada company building one half of a bridge without the other half being constructed by such persons as may receive authority for the purpose from the American congress or from a state legislature.
As regards my hon. friend's argument, that if the state of New York is to be consulted the province of Ontario should also be consulted, I quite agree that, in the first place, this is not a government measure; and secondly, I agree that it is not a political question. But my hon. friend has raised a question of law, and I would point out that the situation on the American side is not the same as that which obtains in Canada, so far as jurisdiction is concerned. The basic principle of our Canadian constitution, as regards the distribution of powers between federal and provincial governments or legislatures, is entirely dissimilar to the principle which governs on the American side. Under the British North America Act, whatever powers have not been expressly given to the provinces belong to the Dominion: on the American side, whatever powers have not been given to the federal government by the states remain in the states. In other words, the residuum of power belongs to this parliament, while in the United States the residuum of power belongs to the states. So that in this matter the state of New York has more extensive powers than has the province of Ontario.
Why?

I explained why. Now,
considering the question in the light of this basic principle, can we say that the province of Ontario has any legislative competence in the matter? It seems to me we must come to the conclusion that it has not. If this federal parliament does not legislate to empower the company to build the bridge, the province of Ontario cannot do so. Even

Niagara Falls Memorial Bridge
if the company applied to the legislature of Ontario, that legislature could take no action. Indeed, even if the province of Ontario itself decided to build the bridge, it would have to come for that purpose to the competent authority, which is this parliament. And this applies not only in international waters; as my hon. friend knows, it applies to interprovincial bridges within Canada. If a company wants to build a bridge between two provinces, neither of those provinces has the power to legislate; the Dominion parliament does so. This principle is not new; it is not unknown in our legislation.
And now as regards the third point raised by my hon. friend, that only this government can declare this work to be in the general interest of Canada. That is an incomplete statement of the law. The government have no such power; as a government they have no legislative power or authority whatever. Under our constitution the government are the executive authority, but the legislative authority is the parliament of Canada, and it is for this house and for the other house to declare if any work is in the public interest of Canada. The government cannot do that.
In conclusion I wish to draw to the attention of my hon. friend the fact that similar acts have been (passed already; this is nothing new. My hon. friend stated to the committee that we were establishing a vicious principle, but in very recent years we passed an act for the construction of the Buffalo and Erie bridge, and the province of Ontario was not consulted for the very good reasons which I have just stated. My hon. friend from Toronto has raised one question; he says that what I aim saying may be true, but on the other hand have we power as a federal govem-met to grant authority for the construction of a bridge on property which belongs to the crown in the right of the province of Ontario?
Who said that?
The Privy Council decided on that the other day.

The point was raised the other day. The only right of the province of Ontario would be to the extent of the park property on which the bridge would rest on the Canadian side, but with all deference, I submit that that question has been settled by the Privy Council in the Rouyn railway case, and also in the Montreal harbour case, to the effect that the federal parliament has such a power. I cannot see how we are interfering with provincial rights at all.
[Mr. Cannon. I
May I ask the Solicitor General if he was referring to me when he spoke of the member for Toronto?
I may be wrong, but I understood my hon. friend to interject a remark about our interfering with provincial property.

Oh, no. If I might, I would explain to the minister the point of my interjection. It was that it carries the matter no further to distinguish between the legislative functions of the provinces and the Dominion on one hand, and of the states and the United States on the other. If the allotment of power in this regard is to the state or to congress, that closes the matter. If it is not alloted to either, the argument of my hon. friend might have some validity, but I do not know that the point arises.

I think the Solicitor
General could not have read section 7. This act is not being passed to authorize the construction of a bridge half way over the river. Section 7 says:
. The company may construct. . . a bridge across the Niagara river for the passage of pedestrians, vehicles, carriages, electric cars or street cars and for any other like purpose, with all necessary approaches, from a point at or near a point between the property of the Canadian National Railways on River road and the north limit of Bender street in the city of Niagara Falls in the county of Welland in the province of Ontario, to a point in the city of Niagara Falls in the state of New York, one of the United States of America, north of the present upper steel arch bridge. ..
Therefore it will be seen that this is not an endeavour to incorporate a company to build a bridge half way across the river, but permission is sought to construct a bridge from a point in Canada to a particular point in the United States. It is also provided as follows:
...but the company shall not commence the actual construction of the said bridge, nor exercise any of the powers hereunder, until an act of Congress of the United States or other competent authority in the United States of America has been passed authorizing or approving the bridging of the said river, but the company may, in the meantime, acquire the lands, submit their plans to the Governor in Council and do all other things authorized by this act.
Therefore we have seen fit to say that this parliament is not at all concerned with the consent of the province of Ontario, but that the bridge must not be constructed until it is approved by the state of New York or the United States of America. I say that is a wrong principle, the people on the Canadian side have a right to be consulted as to whether

Niagara Falls Memorial Bridge
or not their land shall be taken for that purpose, just as the people in New York have to determine whether or not land may be used for this purpose on their side of the river.
But let me go a step further. The Solicitor General referred to the fact that this was in no sense a matter in which the government were interested, but we have observed that while in succeeding sections it is provided that the provisions of the Railway Act shall prevail, in section 7 it is provided that the plans shall be submitted to whom? To the railway commission? No, to the governor in council. And who is the governor in council? The governor in council is the government of the day. Clearly, if this act must go into force, these plans should be submitted to the Board of Railway Commissioners, just as the plans of any railway -which crosses the boundary are submitted. Why should we make the Railway Act apply in succeeding sections but say here that the governor in council shall approve of the plans, a political body as against the commission? Who would come before a committee of this house and ask for the passing of a bill to create a railway company whose plans were to be approved by the governor in council but whose powers were to be regulated by the Railway Act? What is the reason for this distinction? Why have the governor in council in the one instance and the railway commissioners in the other? It seems reasonably clear to me that ii you are going to set up a third power, that power must be the railway commission, which must exercise its authority throughout. You must not make a political body operate in the one instance as against a statutory body in the other. If we are going to pass this statute, at least let us do it as it should be done, making the approval of plans, the determination of routes and matters of that sort, questions to be settled by the railway commission just as though this were a railway.
My main purpose in rising at the moment was to direct attention to the fact that we are authorizing the construction of a bridge going from point to point, from Niagara Falls in one country to Niagara Falls in the other, and that while we have jurisdiction over only half the waterway, we are granting the company power to construct a bridge over the whole distance, although we provide that they can only exercise those powers subject to something else. I submit we should also say that these powers should not be exercised in Ontario unless the people, as represented by the government of this province, are willing and desirous that they should be so exercised. That is the position I desire to make clear.

In answer to my hon.
friend I may say that the jurisdiction of this parliament is also territorial.
It certainly is.
And my hon. friend will never contend that we can legislate out of our own territory.
That is what we are trying to do.

This bill covers the construction of an international bridge. Territorially, our jurisdiction goes to the middle of the river; we must stop there, but we say that that half of the bridge can be built, and that these people cannot exercise their powers until they have received, or until another company has received from the United States authorities, exactly the same powers which we are conferring now upon a Canadian company.
That is not what it says.
When my hon. friend says we are granting power to go on the American side he knows perfectly well that every law passed by this parliament is subject to our territorial jurisdiction.

Perhaps the Solicitor General will tell me if he does not think that under the provisions of the British North America Act this parliament alone has jurisdiction. I understand that to be his contention. On section 4-Capital stock.

This is a clause that should be very carefully considered. Any man familiar with the corporate structure of these enterprises will realize that for the first time in a bill of this character we have capital stock without nominal or par value, and the question suggests itself-on payment of what sum may the company commence operations?

St. Clair Transit Company
Both the Companies' Act and the Railway Act are clear on this point. This section as at present drafted declares only that there shall be 100,000 shares of no par value. Each share, however, shall be of the same value, the issue and allotment of the shares to be made from time ito time for such consideration as may be fixed by the board of directors, by by-law or resolution duly confirmed, which permits the issue of the whole of the common stock for services rendered in getting this charter. Now that is precisely the one thing which this .parliament is endeavouring to stop, and I do think that the law officers of the crown failed to look into the full implications of the section; otherwise they would not have submitted it in its present form. I would certainly prepare an amendment covering this point. Even the Companies' Act itself, when shares are without nominal or par value, provides that the Secretary of State shall insist that a value be given the shares, for the purpose of fees, of not less than so many dollars per share. This section however, permits the whole capital stock to be issued for services rendered in getting the franchise. What we are asked to do in this bill is to create an entity, a transit company; in the second place we are granting it powers; and, thirdly, we are conferring upon the company a franchise which may or may not be valuable, and in regard to which I express no opinion at the moment. But to make the franchise valuable tolls may be imposed, and these tolls are to be approved by the governor in council. I would point out

nnd the Minister of Railways will bear me out-that nothing is so impossible of realization as the satisfactory exercise of these powers by a body like the governor in council, which has no machinery for the purpose. The proper body for the discharge of such functions is of course the Board of Railway Commissioners, whose business it is to deal with matters of this kind, and who have the necessary machinery as well .as experts who may advise them.
It is important, in dealing with this question, that due regard be had to the actual money investment of the enterprise. A few years hence someone may come from Samia -if we build this bridge-and complain that tolls are too high. Thereupon people owning 100,000 shares will come forward and say, "These shares cost us an enormous sum of money, and parliament having recognized that fact, you must not interfere with vested interests and deprive us of dividends to which we are entitled1 in view of the' price we paid." Now, I say, is the time to anticipate any difficulties of this nature. Now is the time to declare that these shares without any nominal
or par value shall have affixed to them, for purposes of the statute, a value of not less than so much per share. The Solicitor General makes provision whereby, on the retirement of the shares, the works created under the authority of the statute fall into possession of the people-of the United States with respect to the American half of the undertaking, and of Canada so far as the other half is concerned. It becomes, therefore, a matter of transcendent importance that we do not deal with watered stock, lest my hon. friends from the west and from other sections of the country as well, say afterwards that what we have done is to give legislative sanction and authority to something which has created a vested interest that must be protected. I know that the Solicitor General is anxious to serve the public interest in this matter and I suggest to him, therefore, that the clause as it now stands is open to the gravest abuse, namely, the issue of the whole capital stock of the enterprise for the purpose of obtaining the franchise. That is exactly what will happen: it has happened times without number in this country. I could show my hon. friends statutes of that kind. subtopic: POSITION ON ORDER PAPER OF MOTIONS AFFECTED BY CLOSING RULE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise t>o a point of order. It is with reference to the transference of the notice of motion given by the bon. member for Rellechasse (Mr. Boulanger), discussed at last Wednesday's sitting, from Notices of Motion to Public Bills and Orders. I have always felt since I have been in this house that the rule laid down in regard to Wednesdays has not been observed in practice; at least it seems to me that the practice has not been in harmony with the rule. Now standing order No. 27 reads thus:
If at the hour of six o'clock p.m. on a Wednesday, or at the time of the adjournment of the house, a motion on the notice paper be under consideration, that question shall stand first on the order paper of the following day, next after orders to which a special precedence has been assigned by rule or order of the house.
It seems to me perfectly clear that under that rule the motions we were discussing last

Wednesday evening when the house adjourned should be first in order of discussion as soon as we reached that particular order of business. I will read further from the rules:
229. It is more favourable to the progress of a motion on the order paper that the debate should not be adjourned on Wednesday at six o'clock, because the motion shall then stand on the order paper for the next day as stated in this rule; if debate is adjourned, the motion * goes to the foot of the orders.
Last Wednesday the debate was not formally adjourned. The house simply rose during the discussion. If we read article 230, we see further:
This rule seems to apply to Wednesday only, the words "or at the time of the adjournment of the house" referring to that day, according to the interpretation given by Bourinot, 3rd edition, pp. 336-337. Its purpose is to keep the motion on the order paper though on Wednesday the house may rise without debate being adjourned because at six o'clock on that day the Speaker adjourns the house without question put. On other days, if debate is not adjourned the question is superseded.
It seems to me that under that rule, where the house adjourns without the debate being adjourned, we would naturally take up the motion of the hon. member for Bellechasse. There is another reference to the same matter-on page 21, section 63, which again deals with the subject as follows:
Bills occupy a more favourable position than motions, which, if the debate is adjourned on Wednesday at six o'clock, go to the foot of the orders. Consequently, it is more favourable to the progress of a motion on the notice paper that the debate should not be adjourned on Wednesday at six o'clock.
The house will notice that at the foot of article 230, it reads:
On other days, if debate is not adjourned the question is superseded.
Therefore it seems that for those who wish to have their motions given full consideration the proper course is that on Wednesday the debate should not be adjourned, while on other days formal adjournment of the debate would appear to be necessary in order that the motion may occupy its proper place on the order paper. That is the only conclusion I can come to from reading these rules. I raise the point of order, therefore, and hold that the motion of the hon. member for Bellechasse should now be the subject of consideration by this house.

The house resumed from February 16, consideration of the proposed motion of Mr. Heaps:
That, in the opinion of this house, the committee on industrial and international relations be authorized to investigate and report on insurance against unemployment, sickness and invalidity.

Mr. Speaker, the motion which is before us this evening is one that was before the house last year, and on that occasion I was pleased with the favourable reception the motion received from members on both sides of the house. Most of the members on the Liberal side were favourable to it, and I was also pleased to see that the hon. gentleman who now occupies the position of leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) spoke in favour of the principles underlying my resolution.
It is rather difficult for any member, or indeed anyone else, to obtain exact data pertaining to the amount of unemployment throughout the Dominion. The Dominion government publish no figures which give anyone a reliable guide as to how much unemployment there really is. In 1926 certain persons endeavoured to make a calculation and they arrived at the conclusion that in the month of December of that year approximately 75,000 people were out of work in the Dominion. This is about the only data that is of value for any one to base an opinion on. The Dominion employment offices throughout Canada have no figures of any value in regard to unemployment.
It has been argued by hon. members as well as by others outside of this house that the question of unemployment is one that should be left entirely to the provinces and the municipalities. I do not agree with that particular viewpoint. I believe unemployment is a problem that ought to be faced by the Dominion government. In this house we deal with and pass legislation that has a direct bearing upon this all-important question. We deal with tariffs, immigration matters, trade treaties, foreign policies, banking laws, and all these I claim affects the volume of employment or unemployment in this country. In our particular legislation that applies to labour, I claim there ought to be some uniformity of action as well as uniformity of
1494	COMMONS
Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Heaps
legislation. If we allowed the provinces to deal with the problem of insurance against unemployment, sickness and invalidity, I presume we would have the same conditions as we have in regard to workmen's compensations acts, mothers' allowances, and so on. We have the spectacle at the present time of a woman living in the province of Quebec, in the city of Hull, let us say, coming across to Ontario and living in Ottawa in order to benefit by certain legislation passed by the Ontario government which is not in effect in the province of Quebec. That merely goes to show the necessity for having uniform legislation in all parts of Canada.
For about four weeks, during the course of the budget debate, hon. gentlemen were discussing the question of unemployment as well as the volume of employment in the Dominion of Canada, and after that debate I do not think that anyone will claim that there is no large volume of unemployment. While hon. gentlemen of the Conservative party claimed that there was a large unemployment problem in Canada, hon. gentlemen of the Liberal party claimed that Canada was in the most prosperous condition since confederation. On the Liberal side they could see nothing but prosperity; on the Conservative side they could see almost nothing but unemployment. While the two viewpoints may appear to be contradictory, I claim that in both there is an element of truth. I claim that we have a large unemployment problem to deal with, and that at the same time there is a good deal of prosperity in this Dominion. What is the cause of this seeming contradiction?
In the year 1917 we had 120,695 more people employed in industry than we had in the year 1924, yet the volume of production was actually greater in 1924 than in 1917. At the same time, in that same period of eight years from 1917 to 1924 inclusive, we had an increased efficiency in individual production of 28 per cent. Taking the year 1910, as compared with the year 1927, we find this remarkable fact:	In 1927, which was a record
year so far as employment was concerned, about 20 per cent more people were employed in industry than in 1910, but during that same period production had increased almost three times.

Are the hon.
gentleman's figures based on the value of production or on units of production?
The volume of production.
Units of production, or the value in dollars and cents?

On the volume as given
by the Bureau of Statistics. You might call that units, if you wish, but I believe the Bureau of Statistics calls it the volume of production. During that period from 1910 to 1927 the production increased almost three times, whereas the number of people employed in industry increased about 20 per cent. In these figures I think you will find one of the main reasons for the unemployment at present existing in the Dominion. We in the Labour movement have no objection to the employment of improved machinery for productive purposes, but what we do object to is that this improved machinery, which ought to bring greater happiness and contentment to the people, does not have that effect. The more labour-saving devices that are introduced into the factories and the greater the volume of production, the greater ought to be the happiness of the people, but what we find is that labour is being displaced, and a greater amount of poverty prevails in the Dominion. At the same time we find on the other hand a greater amount of prosperity. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) said at the time he introduced his budget, the financiers and industrialists in this country claim that prosperity was never greater in Canada than it is at the present time. That was true so far as the financiers and industrialists were concerned; they were really prosperous, but the reason for their prosperity was quite obvious.
If you take the latest figures published by the Bureau of Statistics as to the amount of wages paid to labour, you will find that the amount paid in the year 1924 was approximately the same as in 1917, or to put it in another way, the whole of the benefit of that increased efficiency of the workers in industry went to the industrialists or financiers and practically none of it to the employee; in fact, he is so much the worse off, because he is receiving to-day less for that which he himself produces.

I might add to what the hon. member for Comox-Albemi has said, as to the agitation which exists at present in British Columbia in regard to state health insurance. There has been a very strong demand that something be done in that direction, and meetings of various kinds have been held. I see that the matter was discussed the other day before the Board of Trade Health Bureau in Vancouver by Dr. J. H. MacDermot, whom I believe to be connected with the Vancouver General Hospital. A report of that meeting appears in the Vancouver Daily Province under date of Tuesday, March 8, and from this report it appears that Dr. MacDermot advocated state health insurance and also that, according to his statement, a great many of the medical men of Vancouver favour that plan. He went into details, Which I do not propose to do; suffice it to say that Dr.

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. McQuarrie
MacDermott thought there should be state insurance along the lines of the workmen's compensation scheme whereby contributions should be made and medical service provided for the men who made those contributions: there should be medical assistance for their families, not only in case of sickness but also in the prevention of illness, and the head of the family should receive compensation. This plan was unanimously adopted by the meeting to which I have referred. I might also say that Mr. C. J. Wynn, who is the chairman of the workmen's compensation board of British Columbia, has publicly advocated some similar scheme.
One of the reasons for this agitation in favour of state health insurance is the unfair and arbitrary way in which insurance companies carry on health insurance in this country. Mr. Wynn himself was very badly treated, I believe, and I had a similar experience. I am a firm believer in insurance, and for years have carried almost every kind; I have carried life insurance, fire insurance, accident insurance, health insurance, automobile insurance and burglary insurance.
Has the hon. gentleman carried political insurance?

I have had almost
every kind of insurance, because I believe in it, but I also believe that when I pay my good money for that purpose I should receive protection, and that I should not pay money to any company which is prepared to take that money only so long as it does not suffer a loss. When I find a company which is net prepared to meet a fair loss which it has sustained, then I say it is time something should be done. Now with regard to my own case, as I said, I carried health insurance for years. I had a few small claims, but it was not until last session that I really had a serious illness. I had been carrying a policy in The Employer's Liability Assurance Corporation, supposed to be a very good policy. It is a combination of accident and sickness insurance and covers all diseases or illnesses. It is called a standard disability policy. That policy was taken out by me in July, 1922, and was in renewal of another policy which I had been carrying in the same company for some years. I found that this policy was renewed from year to year as a matter of course.
As long as you were in health.

As long as I did not
make any substantial claim against the company. But last year I had a very serious illness towards the end of the session. It arose 56103-96
to a certain extent in an accidental way, and the original illness that I had was not a serious one at all. I had to submit to a minor nasal operation, but resulting from it I got a very serious infection which laid me up for some time. I had to remain here in Ottawa for quite a long time after the session closed. I had two trained nurses at an expense of $37.50 each per week, and I had to take a nurse with me when I went back to the coast. When I returned to my home I was confined to the house for some time; I was not able to return to my office for several months. Now I thought in the first place that I was covered for one nurse up to the extent of $25 a week because when I took out this insurance policy in the first place I was told that it did provide for a nursing allowance of $25 a week. But the policy itself is misleading in this way: The ordinary individual having been told that much and having received the insurance policy would conclude that he was entitled to a nursing allowance. My claim for nursing allowance was refused. When I first took ill my wife sent a notice to the insurance company advising the agent that I was ill and describing the nature of the illness. The first word I received from the company, before I had put in any claim whatever, was a letter, dated July 22nd, 1927, addressed to myself, and reading as follows:
Dear Mr. McQuarrie:
I have just been advised by head office that they do not wish to renew your accident and sickness policy which expires to-day.
I am very sorry that the company has decided to do this, but they give me no reason whatever.
With appreciation of past favours.
Yours very truly,
J. J. Johnston.
That was before I put in my claim even. They sent me this letter on the very day the policy expired; and mark this: in the face of their repeated renewals, without any request from me from time to time previously when I had not made any substantial claim against them. What was the result? The infection that I unfortunately suffered from was such that my illness might possibly recur. When this company refused to renew the policy I was in this position, that it was impossible for me to get any other sickness insurance. As hon. gentlemen know, when an application is made for insurance of this kind one question that is asked is: Has any company ever cancelled a policy of yours or refused renewal thereof? Well, of course, in my case I had to say, " Yes, the Employers' Liability has refused to renew." As a matter of fact, I had not made any re-

quest for renewal, but the company had, in effect, refused to renew. What did that mean? I tried it out and I found that other sickness insurance companies said: No, under those circumstances we do not think we will give you a policy. I started to enquire into this matter and I found that the same thing had happened to a great many people. There are hon. gentlemen in this house who have had similar experiences, and I suppose there are hundreds, perhaps thousands of people in this country who have been treated the same way that I have been treated. The policy of the sickness insurance companies seems to be that they will take your money if you don't get sick but if you do contract a serious illness they will do one of two things: They will eliminate the disease from which you have suffered or they will refuse to renew your policy. Of course I must admit the policy is one that is issued from year to year, one on which the premiums are paid for one year and the insurance is only for that period. As a matter of law they have a perfect right to refuse to renew your policy, and possibly it would be unfair to require that insurance companies be compelled to issue a policy which would be renewable from year to year up to the time the insured reached a certain age, up to the age of sixty or sixty-five, which I believe is the uninsurable age. But what I say is that no insurance company should be permitted to decline to renew any policy when the insured is at such a stage of health that he is unable to get insurance from any other company. It is true also that before you obtain your money from an insurance company you must give a receipt in Ml for your claim in respect of this particular disease. What I contend is that every insurance company that is carrying on this business should at least be compelled to carry the insured during the time that he is not in a position, by reason of the disease that he incurred during the existence of the policy, to get insurance from any other company.
I promised you, Mr. Speaker, that I would not take up any time unnecessarily, and I do not intend to do so. I think this is a matter that should be investigated by the same committee which the proposer of this resolution has suggested. I beg to move the following amendment which is seconded by Mr. Dickie:
That the said resolution be amended by adding the following:
"That the said committee be authorized to investigate and report on the operations of companies carrying on sickness and accident insurance business in Canada."
Mr. HERlMAS DESLAURIERS (iSt. Mary) (Translation):	Mr. Speaker, I first wish to

congratulate the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps), for the unceasing interest he takes in the labouring classes and for whom I personally have much sympathy.
This resolution embodies one of the most serious problems which, at the present time, bears the stamp of great importance and actuality; it is perhaps the problem that has been foremost in the minds of people all over the world. Pledges of candidates, at election time, numerous publications on the subject, resolutions, measures introduced in legislatures and continuously changed, amended or cancelled, force us to conclude that this problem which exists everywhere is most complex. Its solution is impossible by academic rules and it can only be solved by each individual's thrift and backed by the good will of each and everyone, conditions without which all practical tests of systems have been failures in the past, and will also be in the future.
In Canada, in every province, the problem of invalidity, if we include old people, exists more or less of necessity, owing to the fact that we took part in the -great European conflict. The result was that a great number of old people saw the staff of their old age disappear in the dash of arms on the battlefields. Many saw their sons return disabled, confined to hospitals, adding to the burden of their advanced age; others although unscathed returned home with a different disposition and undesirable habits. A sad state of affairs which spoiled the future of thousands of families. If there is such a thing as -a national conscience, is i't not 'held to compensate its victims, in the greatest measure possible?
Numerous other causes are responsible for invalidity. First old age, lack of natural gifts, want of foresight, trials of life, accidents, illness, forced unemployment, misfortunes, ill luck, these are as many explanations of God's word: "There will always be poor people as there will always be wealthy people". All nations are endeavouring to remedy this evil, without so far having quite succeeded. They have tried to provide for the lack of thrift, by insurances against fire, illness, old age, unemployment, labour accidents, maternity, as -many things encountered along the path of life and ushering its victims towards poverty, when they have not the means of meeting the payments on their insurance policy or do not avail themselves of the advantages they afford when they are able to do so. Many have benefited by insurances. On ithe other hand, owing to uncontrollable circumstances, a great number are unable to take out an insurance, thereby creating the urgent and unavoidable

problem of invalidity which forces governments to act. The legislation should be rather of a preventive and corrective nature, and not one aiming at remedying the effects as they crop up, but having for its objective the removing of the various causes which create invalidity, and therefore tends to reduce the problem to its very minimum.
All the systems advocated heretofore are alike and only differ from one another by the way they are tested. Workmen's superannuation funds in connection with national banks, associations of employers or mutual assistance, are already in existence. They are maintained by the triple contribution of workmen, employers, and the state, and based on the same principles, proceeding in all cases by compulsory insurance or not-according to the countries where the problem is dealt with-and from birth up to the age of seventy. To-day, notwithstanding numerous trials, numerous theories or systems, the problem always remains unsolved, and we must conclude therefore that the rule of thumb has always presided over mutuality and association.
Thrift was not taught by qualified professors, but by too zealous people more or less shrewd, prophets more or less enlightened, heralds more or less interested, with whom method and precision were entirely wanting.
To obtain that end, it is necessary that chairs be founded to take up the study of this difficult science of providing for one's future-for after all is not thrift the economic hygiene of man? Yet the thing does not exist in any country.
Some countries have tried compulsory insurance, for instance Germany, with indefinite results. Others like France advocate optional insurance and obtain insufficient data. Others like Belgium have tried subsidized insurances which gave rise to abuse and injustice. England and Denmark tried the system of supplementary pensions which perhaps would be the system approaching the nearest to the solution of the problem of invalidity if it were supported by the good will of each.
